n: The first of the seven traditional “penitential psalms.” David asks the Lord not to correct him in anger.

f.w: rebuke me not in thine anger

n: He begs for mercy and healing, for he is frail and his bones shake with pain.
His whole self is in anguish. He breaks off mid-sentence: “But you, Lord — how long?”
“Turn back to me, Lord, and rescue me, because of your steadfast love.” He appeals to God’s character, not his own merit.

f.g: Because of your ḥesed — your loyal, covenant love.

n: In death no one remembers or praises God, David argues — so keep me alive to praise you. The Old Testament had a dim view of the afterlife; later revelation fills it out.

f.w: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?

f.g: Hebrew sheol, the place of the dead.

n: Exhausted by groaning, he soaks his bed with tears every night.

f.w: make I my bed to swim
f.g: Flood my bed — vivid exaggeration for intense weeping.

n: His eyes are worn out from grief and grow weak because of all his foes.
Suddenly the tone shifts: “Get away from me, evildoers, for the Lord has heard my weeping!” Jesus uses similar words in the judgment.

f.w: Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity

n: David is now confident: the Lord has heard his plea and accepts his prayer.
His enemies will be ashamed and terrified, and will turn back in sudden disgrace.

f.g: Greatly dismayed — the same word David used of himself in verses 2–3, now turned on his foes.
